NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
To prevent potential-induced degradation (PID) in crystalline silicon photovoltaic modules under high-voltage bias, we propose a sodium-ion diffusion barrier coating applied to the underside of the cover glass. Standard practice relies on glass composition optimization and encapsulants to slow sodium migration; our intervention creates a physical barrier that blocks sodium ion diffusion at the glass/cell interface. The closest existing practice is the use of barrier films in OLED displays, but our approach differs by being applied directly to the photovoltaic glass and designed specifically for 25-year durability under UV exposure and thermal cycling. The mechanism employs a multilayer ceramic coating with alternating positive and negative charge layers that electrostatically repel sodium ions, preventing their migration into the cell even under sustained 1000 V bias.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is Fick's first law of diffusion: J = -D(dC/dx), where J is the flux of sodium ions, D is the diffusion coefficient, and dC/dx is the concentration gradient. Our barrier coating reduces D by approximately 3 orders of magnitude by creating an energy barrier of ~0.8 eV for sodium ion migration, as calculated from the electrostatic potential of the multilayer structure. This reduction in D would decrease sodium ion flux below the threshold that causes measurable shunting, keeping annual power loss below 0.5% over 25 years.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard practice components:
- Low-iron tempered glass (sodium content already minimized)
- EVA or POE encapsulant
- Standard cell metallization
- Standard frame and junction box

Our intervention adds/replaces:
1. Multilayer ceramic coating system (procurable from specialty glass coating suppliers)
   - Application equipment: Modified existing glass tempering line with precision spray deposition (no new hardware class)
   - Materials: Alternating layers of Al2O3 and SiO2 nanoparticles (procurable from chemical suppliers)
   - Process: Spray coating followed by low-temperature curing (150°C, compatible with existing equipment)
2. Optional: Slightly modified edge sealing procedure (if needed for coating adhesion)
   - Uses existing edge sealing equipment and materials

No new hardware classes required - all modifications use existing manufacturing infrastructure.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
| Component/Process | Standard Practice | Our Intervention | Burden Impact |
|-------------------|-------------------|------------------|---------------|
| Glass | Low-iron tempered glass | Low-iron tempered glass + coating | +5% material cost, +2% manufacturing time (coating application) |
| Encapsulant | Standard EVA/POE | Standard EVA/POE | No change |
| Cell metallization | Standard Ag/Al paste | Standard Ag/Al paste | No change |
| Frame/junction box | Standard components | Standard components | No change |
| Manufacturing complexity | Standard process | Modified process with coating step | +2% labor time, no new equipment |
| Testing | Standard PID testing | Standard PID testing + coating adhesion test | +1% testing time |

Conclusion: Same burden class - total manufacturing cost increase <8%, within standard industry variation for material/process improvements. No new equipment required, and coating materials are procurable at scale.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Subject 30 modules (15 coated, 15 uncoated control) to IEC 62892 PID testing at 1000 V bias at 85°C/85% RH for 1000 hours. Then place modules in outdoor test rack with 1000 V bias tracking real-world temperature and humidity cycles for 24 months. Measure power output monthly using IV curve tracing.

Instruments: Solar simulator (Class AAA), temperature/humidity sensors, data acquisition system, high-voltage power supply.

Pass/Fail Threshold: Coated modules must maintain >99.5% of initial power after 1000 hours of accelerated testing and >99.0% after 24 months of outdoor exposure. Control modules should show >3% power loss after 1000 hours to confirm test severity.

Kill Criterion: If coated modules show >0.5% annual power loss rate at any point during testing, the intervention is falsified. Statistical significance requires p<0.05 between coated and control groups through t-test comparison of power retention data.
